title: Ken Paxton Says He’s Tough on Crime. His Trust Invested $600,000 in a Convicted Fraudster’s Company.
author: Zach Despart
content:
Four years after North Texas home builder Scott Sherman completed a federal
prison sentence for mortgage fraud, his new construction materials business
received a $600,000 cash infusion.

The financial boost came from a blind trust set up to prevent [Texas Attorney
General Ken Paxton](https://directory.texastribune.org/ken-paxton/) and his
wife, [state Sen. Angela Paxton](https://directory.texastribune.org/angela-
paxton/), from any overlap in their personal investments and their actions as
elected officials. But previously unreleased records from the attorney
general’s 2023 impeachment investigation show the trust was far from blind and
did not shield the Paxtons from its business dealings, including the
investment in Sherman’s business.

Before long, Wildcatter Sand Services and Grayson County Sand and Gravel,
which Sherman built with his father, grew into a vast enterprise with various
locations and subsidiaries. And along the way, some of those businesses
stopped paying taxes to local governments, including school districts.

But as their tax debts stacked up, Wildcatter companies wired the Paxtons tens
of thousands of dollars in the months leading up to and during the attorney
general’s impeachment on charges of corruption and bribery. Paxton was
eventually [acquitted by the
Legislature](https://www.texastribune.org/2023/09/16/ken-paxton-acquitted-
impeachment-texas-attorney-general/) and is now in an expensive and tight race
for a U.S. Senate seat against Democrat [James
Talarico](https://directory.texastribune.org/james-talarico/), a state
lawmaker.

While Paxton has been in public office for more than two decades, the blind
trust he established upon becoming attorney general has largely obscured his
business dealings. The Paxtons’ investment in Wildcatter through that trust
offers a new, previously unreported look at both the limits of that trust and
the attorney general’s financial association with the very type of business
executives whose prosecutions he typically celebrates.

“In Texas, we fight fraud head-on and will not rest until every last corrupt
actor is brought to justice,” Paxton said in [a news
release](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/news/releases/attorney-general-
ken-paxtons-medicaid-fraud-control-unit-plays-key-role-largest-health-care-
fraud) last year. In a recent social media post linking to a newly released
campaign ad, he wrote, “As Attorney General, I’ve made big pharma and
fraudsters pay billions.”

Doing business with a recently convicted felon undermines that narrative and
erodes public trust in his role as the state’s top anti-fraud watchdog, ethics
experts told ProPublica and The Texas Tribune.

Richard Painter, who served as the chief ethics lawyer for President George W.
Bush, said he would have thought “the attorney general of Texas would have the
good sense not to be dealing with a convicted felon.”

“They’ll pay out their friends while they’re not paying their taxes, run up
debt,” said Painter, who has been critical of staunch Paxton ally President
Donald Trump. “But the question is, why is the attorney general of Texas
dealing with those kinds of people?”

The highlighted section shows an address in Irving, Texas, and a total balance
due of $158,774.10 if paid by August 31, 2024.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-

![A legal court document titled “Order for Tax Warrant” from the 397th
Judicial District Court of Grayson County, Texas. Highlighted text references

property owned by Wildcatter Sand Services
LLC.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/WildcatterSandServicesOrderforTaxWarrant_FAC57E41-2-copy_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)

Wildcatter Sand Services had a tax warrant issued against it for back taxes
after facing a lawsuit by local governments. Obtained and highlighted by
ProPublica and The Texas Tribune

Ken Paxton did not answer detailed questions from the news organizations about
the Wildcatter investment or whether he knew of Sherman’s conviction. He has
previously defended his business dealings, saying he follows ethics laws. A
spokesperson for Angela Paxton, who [filed for
divorce](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/07/10/angela-paxton-divorce-texas-
attorney-general-ken/) last year, said that she was not aware of Sherman’s
criminal history.

Sherman ran a homebuilding firm, Artisan Operating LP, when he pleaded guilty
in 2014 for his role in a [mortgage fraud
conspiracy](https://www.justice.gov/usao-edtx/pr/six-north-texans-indicted-
mortgage-fraud-conspiracy). The scheme involved artificially inflating home
prices to obtain larger loans for more than two dozen properties in cities
across the Dallas-Fort Worth area. Sherman did not respond to calls made to
his cellphone and company or to emailed questions.

Paxton’s connection to Sherman is the second revelation in recent weeks of the
attorney general engaging with people charged with federal crimes. Last week,
The Wall Street Journal reported that Paxton celebrated New Year’s Eve 2024 in
Dubai with two Americans who failed to return to the U.S. after being
[indicted months before on federal healthcare-fraud
charges](https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/ken-paxton-texas-senate-dubai-
trip-b54292c3?st=oBai2R&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink). A spokesperson for
Paxton didn’t address his association with the defendants but said in a
statement to the Journal that the attorney general has been “politically
persecuted for years.”

ProPublica and the Tribune found the Paxtons’ investment in Wildcatter by
reviewing records collected by impeachment investigators.

The records show that Ken Paxton had at least some knowledge of the blind
trust’s investments, which could violate terms the Paxtons set when
establishing the trust.

It would also run afoul of [U.S. Senate
rules](https://www.ethics.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/286a4cf9-5aab-40ef-9a6c-bf2278e79e38/qualified-
blind-trusts-guide---february-2025.pdf#page=5), which Paxton would be bound by
if elected, said Donald Kettl, an ethics expert and former dean of the
University of Maryland’s School of Public Policy. Those rules, Kettl said,
require senators with a blind trust to have no knowledge of its investments.

“It’s reasonable to ask whether a candidate for the U.S. Senate has followed
the ethics rules for financial reporting of blind trusts that would be
required if the candidate became a senator,” he said.

In setting up the blind trust, the Paxtons agreed that their friend Chip Loper
would manage the assets without consulting with them or taking “any
instructions regarding investment matters,” according to incorporation
documents. Loper did not respond to a request for an interview and did not
answer questions about the Paxtons’ involvement in selecting investments.

Text messages that emerged during the impeachment probe, however, showed he
and Ken Paxton discussed certain investments. Mortgage and deed records show
that Paxton purchased eight properties between 2015 and 2026 and then
transferred them into the trust.

The Wildcatter investment also appears to have slipped past the required
firewall.

Angela Paxton served for years on a Wildcatter advisory board beginning in
2022. ProPublica and the Tribune could not find any documents describing her
responsibilities in the role, which she described as “non-governing” on her
personal financial disclosures. While on the board, she voted for legislation
that shielded a subsidiary from certain environmental complaints.

The Paxtons also claimed more than $93,000 in itemized losses from Wildcatter
Sand Services and Grayson County Sand and Gravel on their 2020 federal joint
income tax return.

“That is proof positive that there’s nothing blind about this trust,” said
Kathleen Clark, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis who
specializes in legal and government ethics. If Ken Paxton “can report on his
tax return a transaction, then he is not blind to the transaction.”

### A Board Seat and a Vote

After Wildcatter received the cash injection from the Paxtons’ blind trust,
Sherman went on a shopping spree.

He purchased a sand mine in the North Texas town of Denison and a concrete
plant 40 miles down the road in Gunter, a city of about 2,000 residents. Both
are in Grayson County near the Oklahoma border.

Neighbors complained to Texas environmental regulators about clouds of dust
from Wildcatter and other companies located at the Gunter site that they said
coated their properties for up to 12 hours a day.

In 2021 and 2022, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued
[violation
notices](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28829344-wildcatter-nov/) to
Wildcatter Redi-Mix, the company that runs the Gunter plant. At least one
dust-related violation was resolved when a road leading to the plant was paved
in 2022, according to TCEQ documents. TCEQ did not respond to a request for
comment.

Neighbors continued to raise concerns about the plant.

Angela Paxton joined the advisory board of Wildcatter Materials, which owns
Wildcatter Redi-Mix, a year later. The IRS defines advisory boards as lacking
legal and financial authority over companies. She was still serving on the
board in 2025 as of her last financial disclosure.

Complaints against the company continued. At one point, Gunter resident
Deirdre Diamond, a respiratory therapist and lead advocate for a local group
created to fight pollution from concrete batch plants, reached out to her
representative in the Legislature, then state Sen. Drew Springer.

Despite the TCEQ’s previous violation notices, Springer
[concluded](https://www.texastribune.org/2023/04/17/texas-senate-
bill-471-tceq-complaints-pollution/) that the neighbors’ complaints were
“abusive” and filed [a
bill](https://capitol.texas.gov/BillLookup/Text.aspx?LegSess=88R&Bill=SB471)
that he said at the time would prevent efforts to “weaponize the system.” He
made similar comments in a recent interview with the news organizations.
Springer’s bill allowed the TCEQ to ignore residents after more than five
unsubstantiated complaints in seven years.

Diamond and other opponents believed the bill was an attempt to keep residents
from exercising their rights and argued that the [language was too
vague](https://www.citizen.org/wp-content/uploads/SB-471-TCEQ-complaint-
disregard-Public-Citizen-opposition-with-attachments.pdf). They said the
legislation did not make clear what would constitute an unsubstantiated
complaint and that some complaints may be repeated over the years because of
TCEQ inaction.

When the bill reached the Senate floor, Angela Paxton
[voted](https://journals.senate.texas.gov/sjrnl/88r/pdf/88RSJ04-27-F.PDF#page=21&seqNum=121)
for its passage.

Matt Welch, a spokesperson for Angela Paxton, pointed to the measure’s
bipartisan support in the Senate, saying it was needed “to stop a small group
of environmental activists from wasting taxpayer dollars by weaponizing the
complaint process.”

He said that between 2019 and 2023, the group filed more than 100 complaints
against Dallas-area industrial sites that did not result in findings by the
state environmental agency. “These frivolous complaints divert state resources
from legitimate violations.”

Angela Paxton did not recuse herself from voting on the bill because it did
not relate to any specific company, Welch said. He added that Paxton’s role on
the advisory board “carried no decision-making authority” and that she was
unaware of any complaints or violations against Wildcatter.

Ethics experts said she should have disclosed her relationship with the
company and recused herself. State law bars lawmakers from voting on bills
that benefit them or their businesses. The prohibition does not, however,
apply to legislation that regulates an entire industry, Senate Secretary Patsy
Spaw said.

Because lawmakers write the laws governing what they must disclose and when
they should recuse themselves, “a good amount of the time, the guardrails that
they create for themselves are not enough,” according to Andrew Cates, a San
Antonio ethics lawyer, who said this is one such instance.

Meanwhile, neighbors of Wildcatter’s Gunter plant said the new law left them
demoralized and convinced that lawmakers were not interested in protecting
them or their land. Diamond moved away after the bill passed. She said she
feared the plants’ impact on her children’s health and believed the regulators
were on the side of the company.

She was stunned to learn about the Paxtons’ investment in the company.

“You can’t pretend to be about protecting the people when you directly profit
from it,” Diamond said in an interview.

with Charles A. Loper III as trustee. Six wire transfer deposits under the

Wildcatter Sand Chico LLC totaling $32,347.30.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-

bank statement from the Paxtons’ blind trust checking account shows various

### Wildcatter Helps Paxton in Difficult Times

In the months leading up to the bill passing the Legislature, four Wildcatter
companies wired more than $73,000 to the Paxtons, according to bank statements
reviewed by the news organizations that were part of the previously unreported
impeachment documents.

About $10,000 arrived in the two weeks before Angela Paxton voted on the
environmental bill. An additional $12,000 was wired the week after the
legislation passed in the Senate.

Because the records ProPublica and the Tribune reviewed are limited, the news
organizations cannot say with certainty why the payments were made and how
they were accounted for on the companies’ books.

The payments came as some Wildcatter companies were failing to pay local
property taxes.

At the time, Wildcatter Sand Services, the company the Paxtons’ trust had
invested in, already owed more than $31,000 in back taxes, according to
Grayson County public records.

Several Wildcatter companies also owed hundreds of thousands of dollars in
local taxes in 2023 that soon became delinquent.  

That year, Ken Paxton was facing his own troubles as allegations of bribery
and corruption reached a fever pitch.

Early in 2023, the U.S. Justice Department’s public integrity unit, known for
handling high-stakes political corruption cases, took over an investigation
into allegations by Paxton’s senior advisers that he abused his office. (It
was later dropped in 2025.)

Paxton also reached a tentative $3.3 million settlement with some of those
employees. They had accused him of firing them after they went to authorities
with allegations that he had used his office to go after the enemies of an
Austin real estate investor and donor. The proposed payout required
legislative approval, drawing the ire of lawmakers who questioned why
taxpayers should be on the hook. After the Legislature took no action, a judge
[awarded](https://www.texastribune.org/2025/07/03/ken-paxton-attorney-general-
whistleblowers-appeal/) the whistleblowers $6.6 million in 2025. Paxton called
the ruling a “bogus judgment in support of baseless claims by rogue
employees.”

Some of the Wildcatter payments came while a House committee was investigating
the whistleblowers’ claims about the attorney general’s conduct.  

On May 19, a week before Paxton was formally impeached, the blind trust wired
$9,000 to attorney Mitch Little’s firm. Little later
[represented](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jw6r73SIbsY) both the trust and
Paxton in his impeachment trial. It’s unclear whether the money from
Wildcatter was used to pay for the legal representation. The trust’s checking
account would not have had enough money for that payment without deposits from
the companies earlier in the month, records show. At the time, the trust also
had an investment account with $9,300 in cash and just under $1 million in
securities, but records do not show any distribution from that account to the
checking account in that period.

Neither Loper nor Little, now a state representative, responded to questions
about the transaction. Angela Paxton’s spokesperson said she has no knowledge
of any payments for impeachment lawyers.

Craig Holman, ethics lobbyist for consumer-advocacy group Public Citizen in
Washington, D.C., said it would be particularly problematic if any of the
money was used as a “passthrough” for Paxton’s legal fees.

All told, Wildcatter companies wired the Paxtons’ trust 15 payments between
January and June 2023 totaling more than $83,000. It is unclear whether
payments continued after that date because the records collected by
impeachment investigators ended in June.

The following year, two of those companies became delinquent on nearly
$200,000 in 2023 property taxes to local schools, cities and counties.

The governments had to sue to recover what they were owed.

The post [Ken Paxton Says He’s Tough on Crime. His Trust Invested $600,000 in
a Convicted Fraudster’s Company.](https://www.propublica.org/article/ken-
paxton-investment-scott-sherman-wildcatter) appeared first on
[ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
